title: Inside a memory: register-level read and write
summary: What happens inside a memory when it is written or read? This topic opens a small memory at **register level**: a decoder chooses the word, registers store it at the clock edge, a multiplexer reads it out. You will follow both processes clock by clock, read them in waveforms, and then write the memory structurally and behaviourally in SystemVerilog.
objectives: Name the three parts of a register-level memory.
Follow a write and a read clock by clock.
Read write and read operations in a timing diagram.
Relate the register-level view to an SRAM array.
Write the memory structurally and behaviourally in SystemVerilog.

subsections.title: A memory is registers, a decoder and a multiplexer

steps.title: The parts
steps.md: Decoder, registers and read multiplexer. All registers hold 00.

steps.title: Decode
steps.md: we = 1 and waddr = 2: the decoder raises **word_en[2]** only.

steps.title: Clock edge
steps.md: At the rising edge, register 2 loads din = 0x5A.

steps.title: The others
steps.md: All other registers had their enable at 0 and kept their values.

blocks.title: An SRAM does the same — with cells instead of flip-flops
blocks.md: The **row decoder** of an SRAM is the write decoder, the **word line** is the word enable, the **cells** are the registers, and the **column mux plus sense amplifiers** are the read multiplexer. Only the circuit technique differs.

steps.title: Asynchronous read
steps.md: raddr = 2: the multiplexer passes register 2 to its output after a short combinational delay — no clock needed.

steps.title: Synchronous read
steps.md: An **output register** behind the multiplexer captures the value at the next clock edge: the data arrives one clock later (read latency 1), but the timing is clean and predictable.

blocks.caption: Two ways to read

blocks.md: The same two operations as a timing diagram — learn to read it, every memory datasheet uses this form:

blocks.caption: Cycle 1 writes 0x5A into word 2; cycle 2 reads word 2. Note when each signal changes.

items.title: Why does word 2 change only after the edge?
items.md: Registers sample their input at the rising edge. During the write cycle the enable and the data are prepared; the edge at the end of the cycle stores them.

items.title: Why is the synchronous output one cycle later than the mux output?
items.md: The mux output is ready during the read cycle; the output register samples it at the next edge.

items.title: What if we read and write the same word in one cycle?
items.md: The asynchronous read shows the old value until the edge, then the new one. A synchronous read samples at the edge and therefore gets the **old** value — the read-first behaviour of Topic 5.

blocks.md: The register-level memory written **structurally** — decoder, registers and multiplexer as separate pieces of code:
The **behavioural** version describes the same hardware in four lines. Synthesis builds the decoder and the multiplexer from the array index:

blocks.code:
logic [7:0] word [4];
always_ff @(posedge clk) if (we) word[waddr] <= din;   // decoder + registers
assign dout_async = word[raddr];                        // read multiplexer
always_ff @(posedge clk) dout_sync <= dout_async;       // output register

blocks.title: Use the behavioural style
blocks.md: Both versions give the same hardware. The structural one shows **what** is built; in real designs the behavioural style is shorter, easier to read and lets the tools map large arrays onto SRAM or block RAM.
